🎓 Marketing Fundamentals · Lesson 4 of 5

The Funnel vs the Brand: How Content Really Turns Into Sales

8 min read · Updated November 2026 · Free · Written for Kenya
Share: WhatsApp X Facebook Telegram LinkedIn

At any moment, most people who will one day buy from you aren't ready to buy yet. Research on business buyers puts it at roughly 95 out of 100.

That's why hard-selling every post feels like shouting into the void. There are two big schools of thought on what to do about it. Smart marketers use both.

School 1: the funnel

The funnel idea goes back to AIDA (Attention, Interest, Desire, Action), usually credited to adman E. St. Elmo Lewis in the 1890s. Today it's often drawn as awareness, consideration, conversion and loyalty, with different content for each stage.

StageJob of the contentContent that does itNumber to watch
AwarenessGet noticed by strangersShort videos, trends done your way, relatable humourReach, non-follower views
ConsiderationEarn trust and answer doubtsTutorials, before/after, prices in KES, FAQsSaves, profile visits, follows
ConversionMake buying easy nowOffer posts, WhatsApp link, M-Pesa till, deadlines that are realDMs, orders
LoyaltyBring buyers back and get referralsThank-you posts, customer features, WhatsApp updatesRepeat orders, referrals

School 2: How Brands Grow. Byron Sharp and the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute argue that people don't march neatly down a funnel. Brands grow mainly by reaching more buyers, especially light and occasional ones, and by building mental availability (coming to mind when a need arises) and physical availability (being easy to buy).

✗ MYTH

Growth comes from turning a few followers into superfans.

✓ REALITY

Sharp's double jeopardy pattern: smaller brands have fewer buyers, and those buyers are also a bit less loyal. Growth mostly comes from reaching more people. Loyal fans matter, but for a small brand they usually follow growth rather than cause it.

The bridge. Les Binet and Peter Field studied hundreds of IPA effectiveness case studies and found two kinds of effect: brand building (slow, broad, emotional, lasts) and sales activation (fast, targeted, fades). Their often-quoted optimum is about 60:40 brand to activation, confirmed at 62:38 in a 2018 follow-up.

The debate, fairly

Critics note that half of a set of winning IPA cases showed clear targeting, which cuts against 'reach everyone'. Mark Ritson's answer is 'bothism': use brand and performance together, with the mix set by your situation. 60:40 came from big advertisers, so for a small Kenyan business treat it as a direction, not a formula.

💡 What most creators miss

Mental availability is built around buying moments, which Ehrenberg-Bass calls category entry points. A cake page shouldn't just post cakes; it should own moments like 'kid's birthday this Saturday', 'office send-off' and 'graduation week'. Each moment is a content series.

📋 One-week content mix (roughly 60:40)
BRAND (memory, reach) – 3 posts:
• [BUYING MOMENT] story: '[SITUATION]? Here's how we handled it for [CUSTOMER TYPE].'
• Behind the scenes with your signature look, sound or catchphrase
• A useful tip for the whole category, not just buyers

ACTIVATION (sell now) – 2 posts:
• Offer: [PRODUCT] KES [PRICE], order on WhatsApp [LINK] until [REAL DATE]
• Proof: customer result + 'DM [KEYWORD] to book'
✅ Do this today (under 15 minutes)
⚡ Quick check

Binet and Field's famous 60:40 split refers to what?

It's brand building versus sales activation, based on IPA case studies. Brand work builds memory that makes later selling cheaper; activation cashes it in. Adjust the mix to your situation.

🧠 Key takeaways
  1. Most future buyers aren't ready today, so build memory as well as making offers.
  2. The funnel is a useful map for content jobs; growth mostly comes from reaching more buyers.
  3. Balance brand and activation. 60:40 is a guide from big advertisers, not a law.
  4. Plan content around buying moments, not just products.
